comments.author: sqeaky
comments.story_title: Add a const here, delete a const there
comments.why_zh: 展示每一步的汇编，以及 const 和 constexpr 消除的函数。
comments.quote_zh: 他在很多步骤都展示了生成的汇编，并演示了当正确使用 const（以及后来的 constexpr）时，有多少函数被完全消除。
comments.text_zh: 我觉得这种看法已经过时了。就算 const 属性在某种程度上被破坏却没有产生错误，大多数编译器（至少 GCC 和 Clang）仍会假定代码是符合标准的，并按照标准允许的方式做优化。当你用提到的那个指针去修改本应是 const 的东西时，这可能会导致未定义行为。想想 CppCon 2016 那个演讲里展示的优化量：[VIDEO] 演讲者 Jason Turner 一行行地写代码，并为 Commodore 64 做交叉编译。他在很多步骤都展示了生成的汇编，并演示了当正确使用 const（以及后来的 constexpr）时，有多少函数被完全消除。CppCon 2016 还有很多其他精彩演讲，包括一个讲 const 以及它带来哪些优化可能的，还有几个讲编译器如何更愿意通过让不符合标准的代码行为未定义来“弄坏”它们。这些其实都不算惊人也不新鲜，除非你一直是在针对某个编译器实现写代码，而不是针对标准写代码。
comments.text: I think this way of looking at it old. Even if the const-ness is somehow subverted without generating an error then most compilers (or at least GCC and Clang) will presume the code is compliant and make optimizations following what the standard allows. This potentially results in undefined behavior when that pointer you mentioned is used to modified a thing that ought to be const. Consider the amount of optimizations seen in the video from CppCon 2016: [VIDEO] Jason Turner, the presenter, is writing code a few lines at a time and cross compiling for the Commodore 64. He shows his assembly at many steps of the way and shows how many functions are completely elided when const (and later constexpr) are used correctly. There are a ton of other good talks from CppCon 2016 including one about const and what optimizations it makes possible and several about how compilers are more willing to "break" code that is non-compliant by making its behavior undefined. None of it really shocking or new, unless you have been writing to one compiler implementation instead of to the standard.

comments.author: mrkeen
comments.story_title: What is the case against F#? (2009)
comments.why_zh: 脚注引用 C++17 在 Commodore 64 上运行。
comments.text_zh: C 能很好地映射到机器上。（底层程序员大概会为此把我钉上十字架。）但就拿它缺少闭包这一点来说。闭包要么需要某种内存管理，要么需要巧妙的程序变换，而到那一步，你就失去了只有栈和堆的那种简洁性。尽管像我这样的一代 Java 程序员从小就认为 C++ 是老古董、Java 是它的天然继承者，但在 lambda、泛型、类型层面的各种花招方面，C++ 一直悄悄地领先于 Java。更不用说性能和向后兼容性了 [1]。但读 C++ 会让我的眼睛流血。做业务逻辑和 Web 应用开发，我更喜欢函数式编程。Haskell 很快，但它不是 C++，这也没关系。我并不想让 Haskell 去抢 C/C++ 的市场份额。我希望它去和那些给不了我性能、安全性或简洁性的语言竞争。[1] C++17 跑在 Commodore 64 上：[视频]
comments.text: C maps to the machine well. (Low-level programmers will probably crucify me for that.) But take its lack of closures as an example. Closures require either some kind of memory management, or clever program transformations, at which point you lose the simplicity of just having the stack and heap. As much as a generation of Java programmers (like myself) grew up thinking that C++ was old hat and Java was its natural successor, C++ has been quietly ahead of Java with regard to lambdas, generics, type-level trickery. Not to mention performance and backward-compatibility [1]. But reading C++ makes my eyes bleed. I much prefer FP for business logic and web-app development. Haskell is fast but it's no C++, and that's OK. I wouldn't want Haskell to take C/C++ market-share. I want it to compete against other languages that don't give me performance, safety or terseness. [1] C++17 on the Commodore 64: [VIDEO]

comments.author: Marcus10110
comments.story_title: Motorola 6800
comments.why_zh: 关于 i386 到 6502 翻译器的演讲启发了 6800 fork。
comments.quote_zh: 看完 Jason Turner 在 CppCon 上关于编写 i386 到 6502 汇编翻译器的演讲之后
comments.text_zh: 我身后架子上就有一台 ET-3400！前几天我还在玩它。看完 Jason Turner 在 CppCon 上关于编写 i386 到 6502 汇编翻译器的演讲 [1][2] 后，我开始做一个以 6800 为目标的 fork。我只让大约 3 条指令跑通了，但对于一些把优化开到最大的非常简单测试代码来说，这其实就够了。另外，有人专门为 ET-3400 trainer 写了一个很棒的模拟器 [3]，我成功让自己的应用在上面跑起来了！[1] [VIDEO] [2] [LINK] [3] [LINK] 对我来说，写现代 C++ 并把它编译到那么早期的微处理器上，这个想法有种特别之处。不过 512 字节 RAM 是个相当大的限制。我想过用 Arduino 或 FPGA 来模拟 EEPROM，但项目卡住了。我时不时会翻翻 LLVM 后端文档，但好像一直没法下定决心去尝试写一个后端。
comments.text: I have an ET-3400 on the shelf behind me! I was just playing with it the other day. After watching Jason Turner's CppCon talk on writing an i386 to 6502 assembly translator [1][2], I started working on a fork that would target the 6800. I only got about 3 instructions working, but that's really all you need for some really simple test code with optimization turned to the max. It also turns out that someone wrote a fantastic emulator specifically for the ET-3400 trainer [3], and I managed to get my application running on it! [1] [VIDEO] [2] [LINK] [3] [LINK] There is something special to me about the idea of writing modern C++, and compiling it for such early microprocessors. The 512 bytes of RAM is a pretty big limitation though. I wanted to try and emulate an EEPROM using an Arduino or FPGA, but got stalled out on the project. From time to time I like to browse through the LLVM backend documentation, but I can't seem to commit to trying to build a backend.
